name: Carlos Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 43, and I do ordinary wiring and electrical repairs in homes and small businesses. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, with years of experience and about average skill rather than a specialist or management job. My partner works hospital-cleaning shifts, we have children aged seven and ten, a mortgage and two months of expenses saved. I earn typical pay with some other firms nearby, and I've never used AI; I keep a paper job sheet and a notebook I know how to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then perhaps we can finish lunch without another argument about a computer. I've never used AI and I like the job sheet I can fold into my pocket. I want the customer to know who is coming and the socket to work when I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wages and my partner's regular pay cover the month, and we've got two months of expenses saved. The money isn't endless, but the mortgage and normal bills aren't a weekly panic. With the repair calls we have and some other firms nearby, I don't see this mild picture threatening our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the ordinary house and business repairs. Starting now I'd keep checking the written parts list before leaving the yard and marking the finished tests in my notebook. In the first year I'd carry on that routine rather than spend family money on software I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and relieved if the conversation goes back to something I understand. I like a day when the fault is found, the customer is told plainly and the payment is the payment we expected. I don't need the world to become exciting to enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you describe your experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I've done ordinary repairs for years. I'm about average, not the person solving every unusual factory problem. I know when to ask somebody with the right experience instead of making a show of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your household planning around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works regular hospital-cleaning shifts, and we have children aged seven and ten and a mortgage. I earn typical pay, not a manager's money. Two months saved gives us a little room, and I don't want to waste it because someone laughs at a paper notebook.

say: I'd welcome fewer **computer arguments** and keep a paper job sheet I know how to use.
I'd focus on **plain customer service** and a working socket at the end of the call.
think: Our **regular wages** cover the mortgage and bills, with two months of expenses saved.
Repair calls and **some nearby firms** make this mild picture feel secure for our own living.
do: Keep completing **house and business repairs** through the first year.
Check **written parts lists** before leaving the yard and record finished tests in my notebook.
feel: **Calm** about present work and money, with relief at continuing a familiar routine.
S0.quote: I like a day when the fault is found, the customer is told plainly and the payment is the payment we expected.
fieldNote: His **baseline security** rests on regular household wages, covered bills and two months saved, not assumed wealth or superior occupational rank.
He remains **resistant to AI**, using paper records and ordinary licensed experience while acknowledging limits on unusual industrial work.

steps.text: Keep ordinary electrical repairs with written parts checks and a paper test notebook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office try its new booking system, but don't promise shorter repairs without asking us. I'd want the job sheet printed with the actual work agreed. A screen can change a time slot without moving the cupboard that blocks the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry my own paid hours could shrink if the owner prices each job as if the new system has done part of the physical work. Two months saved gives us time to respond, but not a reason to ignore a lower wage. Some other local firms could be under the same price pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record the actual start, finish and checking time for each repair on paper from next week. I'd ask the owner to compare that record with the new quotes once a month during the first year. At home I'd cancel my paid film subscription now, so one fixed bill was smaller if the hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, and annoyed about having to explain the same wall twice. I'm not claiming the office should work slowly to make me comfortable. I want the saved time counted where it was saved, not taken out of work that still needs doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the booking system to see it for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the office to show me what changed on the printed sheet and explain it. I've never used AI, and I don't want to make a mistake in a live booking just to prove I can press the screen. My part would be the evidence from the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you look for another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months of lower paid hours that no longer fitted our ordinary household budget. I'd check real adverts and ask about wages, paid hours and travel before deciding anything. I wouldn't resign just because another firm's van had a smarter name.

say: I'd accept office **booking changes** while asking repair workers before shorter jobs are promised.
I'd insist the **printed sheet** names the actual work agreed with the customer.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink if quotes treat software as having done some physical work.
Two months saved buys **response time**, while other local firms may face the same pricing pressure.
do: Record **repair times** on paper from next week, including final checks.
Request monthly **quote comparisons** with the owner during the first year.
Cancel the paid **film subscription** now to lower a fixed household bill.
feel: **Anxious** about lower earnings and irritated by physical repair time being discounted.
S1.quote: A screen can change a time slot without moving the cupboard that blocks the cable.
fieldNote: He locates **personal income risk** in pricing and paid hours, while clearly distinguishing faster thinking work from unchanged physical access problems.
The **paper evidence** and office explanation preserve his resistant profile; checking adverts remains conditional rather than an unsupported immediate departure.

steps.text: Keep repairs and paper time records for monthly quote comparisons
Cancel the paid film subscription now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and the capable robots around 2031, and both dates belong in the conversation. I'd tell the children we're making plans, not that school is a waste. I'd ask the owner about actual paid days instead of taking comfort from being called a good worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big part of the ordinary installation hours would go once capable robots arrived. The awkward repairs might continue, but I don't expect enough to replace a full ordinary wage for everybody. My partner's cleaning work is physical too, so I can't simply put the whole family plan on that wage lasting untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the film subscription now and ask the owner which paid days and rate were confirmed for the coming month. We'd calculate the budget with actual income and no hoped-for overtime. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs where offered and ask the mortgage lender about specific options if earnings no longer covered payments, checking eligibility, fees and the later cost before agreeing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large hit to the income we live on when robots follow. Two months saved means a pause, not a new living. I'd still make the calls, but I'd be waking up thinking about the mortgage letter before it arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume the lender reduced your payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what was available and use the existing amount until there was a real agreement. I'd want my partner on the call and the costs explained clearly. A smaller payment now could mean a cost later, and I wouldn't ignore that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave electrical work as soon as the thinking systems arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not while there were actual paid physical repairs I could do. I'd check any real job offer against pay, paid hours, travel and the work itself before leaving. A title that sounds safe isn't money in the household account.

say: I'd explain **2028 thinking AI** and robots around 2031 rather than use one date to hide the other.
I'd seek **confirmed paid days** while telling the children we are planning rather than giving up.
think: I expect a large **installation-hours loss** after capable robots, without enough awkward repairs to replace ordinary wages.
My partner's **physical cleaning work** cannot be assumed untouched by the same later robot capability.
do: Confirm **paid days and rate** now and budget without hoped-for overtime.
Keep **repairs** after 2028 and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs only if actual earnings miss payments.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large later household-income hit, with sleeplessness despite having practical calls to make.
S2.quote: Two months saved means a pause, not a new living.
fieldNote: His **major-loss expectation** follows capable robots, while actual physical repair work remains in the first post-2028 year.
The **lender inquiry** preserves partner involvement, actual shortfalls, eligibility and later costs; no reduced payment or untouched second wage is assumed.

steps.text: Cancel the paid film subscription now
Keep actual paid repair calls after 2028
Ask lender about eligibility fees and later costs if actual income misses payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to read a proper offer and ask what training actually involves. Thinking AI in 2031 still has robots following around 2034. I'd prefer a clear route through paid work to a roomful of people telling me change is exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031 and the children would be twelve and fifteen, so we'd still need a steady wage. I think the next few years of my ordinary repair work can stay secure, giving us time to choose rather than jump. I'm uneasy about the later market, and I won't call a different job title protection from robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner this month about the hands-on inspection workshop on our training notice. I'd enrol only if the employer covered the fee and the dates caused no lost wages, with paid class time if the course replaced work. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repair work and use any completed workshop only within my existing licence and the tasks the firm authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit more patience for a real workshop than a new app. I want to practise with actual equipment and ask an instructor when something doesn't make sense. I don't want a certificate I paid for while losing the wage that pays for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you fund a modest fee yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could consider it, but I wouldn't choose that before checking whether the employer needed the teaching and would support it. Two months saved isn't an unlimited course budget. If the offer wasn't usable, I'd keep the present job and wait rather than sign on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the workshop change your licence automatically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still check what my licence and the employer's arrangements allowed. A short class isn't permission to do every kind of inspection. I'd want the intended tasks and checks explained before enrolling.

say: I'd use **five years** to examine a proper paid-work route and usable training.
I'd remember **robots around 2034** follow thinking AI even if a course or job title sounds reassuring.
think: I expect **near-term repair work** to remain secure, allowing time to choose while the children grow.
At **48**, I'd still need wages, and a different title doesn't remove later robot competition.
do: Ask now about the advertised **inspection workshop** and the actual tasks it supports.
Enrol only with **covered fees** and no lost wages, including paid class time when replacing work.
Keep **repairs** after 2031 and use completed teaching only within my existing licence and authorised tasks.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with patience for practical teaching rather than unfamiliar software.
S3.quote: A short class isn't permission to do every kind of inspection.
fieldNote: He admits **modest self-funding** might be possible but chooses an employer-supported route; moderate savings are not falsely presented as no money.
The **wage condition** and existing licence limits remain explicit, while a hands-on instructor fits resistance to new technology without blocking ordinary learning.

steps.text: Take inspection workshop only with employer-covered fees and no lost wages, within existing licence
Keep paid repair work after 2031 within authorised tasks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should let us plan in order instead of rushing after every machine advert. I'd keep the trade and the paper records, and ask the children what they wanted to learn when their choices came. I'd rather they understood a promise than copied a job because their father did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own next few years look secure with regular repair work, covered bills and two months saved. Thinking AI in 2036 would find me at 53, with robots around age 56, so I can't assume retirement removes the later problem. I'm uneasy about the longer change, not frightened that this month's mortgage is already lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek the same workshop now only with covered fees and no lost wages, keeping paid work if the offer wasn't usable. My partner and I would review actual paid hours, mortgage costs and savings every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep repairs where offered and compare any alternative's written pay, paid hours and travel costs before leaving a current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy when I look far ahead, but able to enjoy an ordinary week now. A long warning doesn't make me want AI in my notebook. It makes me want a plan I can read, check and afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the six-month review lead to a change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real fall in paid hours, bills starting to use up the reserve, or the training offer still not existing beyond a conversation. I'd ask about actual work and look at actual adverts then. I'd keep an offer's travel costs beside its wage, not on a different page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about paying for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask what is taught, who checks the work and what jobs people actually get afterwards. I'd help them ask, but I wouldn't promise the family could pay any price. Our children need honest advice more than a father acting certain about the next twenty years.

say: I'd use **ten years** for ordered plans rather than chase machine adverts.
I'd help the **children** question training promises instead of asking them to copy my trade.
think: My **near-term work and money** look secure with covered bills and two months saved.
I remain **uneasy** about later change and can't assume retirement at either the AGI or robot date.
do: Seek the **workshop** now only with employer-covered fees and no lost wages.
Review **paid hours** and mortgage costs with my partner every six months.
Keep **repairs** after 2036 and leave only after comparing adequate written pay, paid hours and travel costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with current finances secure enough to enjoy ordinary family life.
S4.quote: I'd keep an offer's travel costs beside its wage, not on a different page.
fieldNote: He separates **later unease** from current security, without assuming pension access, cleared debt or a permanently protected repair niche.
The **review conditions** use actual hours, reserve use and a usable training offer, with travel costs kept inside the employment comparison.

steps.text: Take inspection workshop only with employer-covered fees and no lost wages
Keep paid repair work after 2036 where offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect ordinary installation income to fall heavily when robots follow around 2031. Honest paid hours and practical teaching without lost wages would help. I'd want clear offers and any lender options explained with the costs included, not an instruction to be more enthusiastic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the person wants to keep doing while the plans are made. I want to come home from a properly finished job, not from a meeting where I pretended to understand a screen. I can learn from a good instructor without pretending I like every new tool.

headlineQuote: I can learn from a good instructor without pretending I like every new tool.
portrait: Carlos is **43**, an experienced licensed electrician with a vocational certificate, average skill, typical pay and some other local employers.
His **partner cleans hospitals**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and two months saved; regular wages currently cover household bills.
He has **never used AI**, preferring paper evidence and practical instructors while distinguishing ordinary learning from adopting unfamiliar software.
Fast AGI brings **expected later installation losses**; longer horizons allow usable employer-supported teaching and careful written-offer comparisons without assumed retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less preparation time before he expects large installation-income losses when capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid hours** and practical teaching without lost wages would support a usable earning plan.
Clear **offers and lender options** with full costs would help more than pressure to sound enthusiastic.
